picks.style: late antique river hymn, cithara and low flute with soft water percussion, warm tenor, flowing, celebratory, unhurried
picks.why: 'Hail, river ... O greenest of rivers!' — a direct address that gathers spring, brook, lake and tide into one praise.

picks.style: pastoral idyll, panpipes and light frame drum, mixed voices, playful, sunlit, then hushed at the close
picks.why: Nymphs ducking the Satyrs at noon while nobody watches, ending on the poet refusing to say more — mischief with a veil drawn over it.

picks.style: meditative water song, harp and glassy bowed strings, soft high voice, slow, transparent, drifting
picks.why: Looking down through clear water: the furrowed sand rippling, the pebble that gleams and hides, the gravel setting off green moss.

picks.style: roman satirical prologue, plucked lyre and dry hand percussion, wry conversational baritone, brisk, sardonic, clipped
picks.why: 'I never wet my lips at the nag's spring' — hunger taught the parrot to say good morning, and that is the whole theory of poetry.

picks.style: insistent moral chant, low strings and ticking percussion, urgent tenor, driving, circling, unresolved
picks.why: 'Tomorrow this shall be done.' The same tomorrow it will be done — the rim that turns upon itself and is never caught.

picks.style: stern latin invective, low brass and deep drum, hard declaiming voice, weighty, accusing, building to a curse
picks.why: The prayer against tyrants: let them see virtue, and pine for having forsaken it. The best line Persius ever wrote.

picks.style: renaissance art song, lute and viol, countertenor, gentle, chamber, wintry and aching
picks.why: Sonnet 97 entire — 'How like a winter hath my absence been' — an autumn that feels like December because one person is missing.

picks.style: elizabethan lute song, solo lute and bass viol, warm tenor, unhurried, radiant then clouding over
picks.why: Sonnet 33 entire — the sun flattering the mountain tops, then hidden by the basest clouds, then forgiven.

picks.style: renaissance consort song, viol consort and lute, grave countertenor, slow, embattled, resolving to a single bright line
picks.why: Sonnet 65 entire — brass, stone, earth and sea against time, and only black ink left standing at the end.

picks.style: roman comic aria, tibia and plucked strings, worldly baritone, conversational, quickening, rueful
picks.why: Parmeno's catalogue of love — 'wrongs, suspicions, enmities, reconcilements, war, then peace' — and the folly of being mad with reason.

picks.style: comic patter song, pizzicato strings and woodblock, sly tenor, fast, antithetical, self-delighted
picks.why: The parasite's manifesto: 'Does any one deny? I deny: does he affirm? I affirm.' Built on a rhythm that sings itself.

picks.style: roman narrative song, lyre and soft drum, hushed conspiratorial voice, unhurried, wondering, sensual
picks.why: The boy studying the painting of Danaë's golden shower and delighting that a god would turn himself into money to get in through the roof tiles.

picks.style: english fable ballad, fiddle and plucked cittern, bright storytelling tenor, brisk, four-beat, wry
picks.why: 'Twofold's the genius of the page, to make you smile and make you sage' — a prologue that states its own terms, then walks straight into the wolf and the lamb.

picks.style: comic beast fable, harpsichord and tabor, mocking mixed voices, trotting, strophic, punchline-timed
picks.why: The jackdaw in borrowed peacock quills, stripped by both flocks and told he should have stayed at home. A complete fable with its sting intact.

picks.style: dry epigrammatic air, plucked lute and light percussion, deadpan baritone, measured, ironic, clipped
picks.why: The cock finding a pearl on the dunghill and preferring a grain of barley, closing on 'to whom in vain my pearls are thrown.'

picks.style: persian-inflected art song, santur and low strings with soft frame drum, dark warm voice, slow, fatalistic, circling
picks.why: Rubaiyat quatrains at their bleakest: the phantom caravan reaching the Nothing it set out from, and the door with no key.

picks.style: island elegy, acoustic guitar and low flute, weathered male voice, unhurried, salt-worn, valedictory
picks.why: 'A darkening sky and a whitening sea' — a man writing his own epitaph on a stone from the grey sea wall.

picks.style: victorian hymn-lament, chamber organ and viola, plaintive alto, slow, questioning, unresolved
picks.why: 'That the mark of rank in Nature is capacity for pain, and the anguish of the singer marks the sweetness of the strain' — a whole thesis in one stanza.

picks.style: greek self-mocking lyric, lyre and hand drum, dry knowing male voice, moderate, ironic, conversational
picks.why: Solon quoting his own critics — the fool who would not haul in a net full of fish — and answering with a flayed pouch and a blotted line.

picks.style: greek gnomic chant, plucked lyre and low drone, steady grave voice, measured, plain, resolute
picks.why: 'Our virtue for their wealth — since one abides always, while riches change their owners every day.'

picks.style: elizabethan broadside lament, bowed lyre and tabor, grim baritone, measured, foreboding, plain
picks.why: 'These iron times breed none that mind posterity' — and the patent-holder's boast: if the mills go up, down go the goodly trees.
